chapterTitle: Troubleshooting Common Routing and Switching Issues
aiGenerationNote:
Create a 15-minute case study video. Present five distinct troubleshooting scenarios: OSPF adjacency, BGP route advertisement, VLAN trunking, STP loop, and firewall filter drop. For each scenario, start with a problem description and a simplified network diagram. Then, walk through the diagnostic steps using specific Junos CLI commands (e.g., `show ospf neighbor`, `show bgp summary`, `show interfaces <trunk>`, `show spanning-tree`, `show firewall filter <filter-name> counter`). Show the expected output and explain how to interpret it to identify the root cause. Conclude each scenario with the specific Junos command to fix the issue. Use split-screen for diagrams and CLI. Include a final interactive quiz asking learners to identify the correct troubleshooting command for a given problem.

screens.title: Troubleshooting Common Routing and Switching Issues
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter we focus on practical troubleshooting patterns you will use every day with Junos devices. You will learn to form a hypothesis, collect evidence with show commands, inspect control-plane exchanges like OSPF LSAs and BGP TCP sessions, and validate fixes. For example, if an OSPF neighbor is stuck in ExStart, the immediate checks include interface status, MTU, area ID, and firewall filters blocking multicast. Each technique pairs a command such as show ospf neighbor, show interfaces extensive, or monitor traffic with a reasoning step that tells you what to expect. We emphasize common misconceptions too — for instance, missing routes in the RIB are not always a routing-protocol bug; they can be the result of passive interfaces, export policies, or implicit deny in firewall filters. By the end of these lessons you'll be able to triage adjacencies, peering, trunk mismatches, STP roles, and filter term order confidently and document the fix. Start by learning the core checks and commands, then practice the scenario-based steps to build reliable troubleshooting muscle memory.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: This chapter trains you to diagnose and resolve the most frequent routing and switching faults on Juniper gear. First, you will learn to detect and fix OSPF adjacency and LSA issues — for example, recognizing the impact of an MTU mismatch or a passive interface on adjacency formation. Second, you will be able to bring up BGP peers reliably by verifying TCP reachability, AS numbers, and update-source settings, and by checking policy-based import/export mistakes. Third, you will verify VLAN membership and trunk configuration to restore inter-VLAN traffic and fix native VLAN mismatches that silently drop traffic. Fourth, you will inspect Spanning Tree behavior to identify incorrect root bridge election or blocked ports causing unexpected paths. Each objective pairs concrete Junos commands with a troubleshooting mindset so you can find the root cause quickly and test your fixes. A common misconception is to change configuration without first validating control-plane evidence; these objectives emphasize collecting show output and forming a hypothesis before committing a fix.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Applied Skills
screens.narratorSegment: Beyond the core protocol checks, this chapter teaches supporting skills that make troubleshooting effective and repeatable. You will learn to examine Junos outputs such as show ospf database to verify LSAs, show bgp summary to confirm TCP sessions, and show security flow session to observe SRX session state. You will practice adding counters to firewall filter terms and using monitor traffic to capture packet-level evidence. Another objective is to form a clear hypothesis and document the findings and the fix — a habit that reduces repeat incidents. For example, after resolving a native VLAN mismatch you should record the original trunk settings, the corrective set command, and the verification output. A common misconception is to rely solely on a single show command; we stress combining multiple outputs — interface, protocol, and policy — to paint an accurate picture before committing changes.

Module 8 › Chapter 8.8 › Applied Skills
Applied Skills
Commands, captures, counters, and documentation practices
Junos Evidence
  • Use show ospf database for LSA completeness and show ospf overview for router IDs.
  • Use show bgp summary for session state and monitor traffic to test TCP 179 reachability.
Filter & Counting
Add count counters to suspect firewall terms and observe hits with show firewall filter <name> counter to confirm packet matches.
Monitoring
Use monitor traffic interface <if> matching "tcp port 179" to validate BGP TCP connectivity during triage.
Document
Capture pre-change output, the corrective set commands, and post-change verification to complete the troubleshooting record.

screens.title: OSPF adjacency stuck states and first checks
screens.narratorSegment: When an OSPF neighbor fails to reach Full, start by defining the claim: adjacency formation requires IP connectivity, matching area IDs, compatible network types, identical authentication and MTU, and that nothing in the path blocks OSPF packets. A concrete example is an adjacency stuck in ExStart. ExStart often points to an MTU mismatch preventing Database Description exchange. To check, run show interfaces <interface> detail and compare MTU on both peers; also confirm interface is up/up. Then run show ospf neighbor to observe the state and show ospf database to review LSA exchange progress. Another common cause is passive-interface misconfiguration: passive prevents Hello exchange and LSA propagation. If neighbors are configured with different network types — for instance one side set to point-to-point and the other left as broadcast — adjacency can fail or remain in 2-Way. Also confirm firewall filters are not blocking OSPF multicast addresses 224.0.0.5 or 224.0.0.6. A typical remediation sequence is: validate interface and MTU, remove unintended passive, set matching interface-type, and then clear ospf neighbor or reset the interface to force reformation. Misconception check: do not change area IDs or authentication without collecting evidence; that can create new failures. Takeaway: verify MTU and interface settings first, then inspect LSA and neighbor states.

keyIdea.text: MTU mismatch, passive interfaces, area or network-type mismatch, authentication differences, and filters are primary causes; always validate interface MTU and show ospf neighbor first.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.8 › OSPF Adjacency
Troubleshooting steps
A compact checklist you can follow when an adjacency is not Full.
Command checks
  • show interfaces <iface> detail — verify up/up and MTU
  • show ospf neighbor — observe adjacency state
  • show ospf database — confirm LSA propagation
  • show configuration protocols ospf area — confirm area and interface-type
Concrete example
Adjacency stuck in ExStart. After show interfaces reveals MTU mismatch, align the MTU on both sides, then clear the adjacency or flap the interface to force DBD exchange.
Common mistake
Changing OSPF area or authentication without capturing neighbor and interface state first can mask the real cause. Always collect evidence first.
Example CLI workflow
show interfaces ge-0/0/0 detail
show ospf neighbor
show ospf database
show configuration protocols ospf area
Example output interpretation
  • If show ospf neighbor shows ExStart, compare MTU values from show interfaces; mismatch prevents DBD exchange.
  • If show ospf neighbor shows 2-Way on a point-to-point link, check network-type mismatches and DR/BDR expectations.
  • If LSAs are missing from show ospf database, verify passive-interface settings and filters blocking multicast.
Key Takeaway

Start with interface and MTU checks, then verify OSPF area, network type, and authentication before changing topology or credentials.

screens.title: Missing or incorrect OSPF routes
screens.narratorSegment: When OSPF routes are missing from the routing table, the problem often lies downstream from adjacency formation: inspect the LSA database, router IDs, and whether interfaces are inadvertently passive. Begin with show route protocol ospf to identify which prefixes were learned and which are absent. Then use show ospf database to see if LSAs for those networks exist locally; missing LSAs indicate the network was never advertised or was filtered. Router ID conflicts can prevent proper LSA acceptance or cause confusing behavior — verify uniqueness with show ospf overview. Passive interfaces stop Hello exchanges and prevent LSA advertisement for networks on that interface; check configuration for unintended passive statements. Another frequent policy-level cause is firewall filters blocking LSAs or multicast addresses 224.0.0.5 and 224.0.0.6. A concrete example: an internal network not appearing because the interface was set to passive in the area configuration. Fix by removing the passive flag for that interface and verifying LSA injection with show ospf database and then show route protocol ospf. Misconception check: a missing OSPF route in the RIB does not always mean the LSA was incorrect — it can be suppressed by policy, rejected by route selection, or overridden by a more specific static route. The takeaway: correlate adjacency, LSA, and policy outputs to find the true cause.

keyIdea.title: OSPF Route Diagnosis
keyIdea.text: Missing routes require checking LSA presence, router ID uniqueness, passive-interface settings, and possible filter/policy interference before applying fixes.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.8 › OSPF Routing
Definition & Causes

When routes learned by OSPF do not appear in the routing table, verify the presence of LSAs, unique router IDs, and that interfaces are not passive. Also check for filters or route policies that modify or suppress routes.

Quick command set
show route protocol ospf
show ospf database
show ospf overview
show configuration protocols ospf area
Example scenario
An IRB network is not advertised because the corresponding interface was accidentally marked passive in the area config. Removing passive allows LSAs to be generated and the route to appear in the RIB.
Misconception
Seeing no route in the RIB does not always mean OSPF failed to advertise; it might be filtered or overridden. Correlate outputs across database, routes, and policies.
Interpretation guide
  • If show ospf database lacks an LSA for the prefix, the origin router did not inject it or a filter prevented it.
  • If show ospf overview shows duplicated router IDs, assign a unique router-id under routing-options.
  • If the interface is passive, remove the passive flag so LSAs are generated and Hellos may be exchanged where applicable.
Key Takeaway

Correlate the RIB, the OSPF database, and interface config; that triad reveals the majority of OSPF route problems.

screens.title: Why BGP sessions fail to establish
screens.narratorSegment: When BGP does not show an Established state, treat the issue as a TCP reachability and configuration verification task. Start by confirming basic reachability with ping to the neighbor IP and by testing TCP port 179 with a packet capture or monitor traffic filter. A common operational check is to ensure the correct AS numbers are configured for each peer; mismatched AS numbers will prevent session establishment. If you use loopback interfaces as update-source, verify that the neighbor reaches that loopback via the control-plane and that update-source is configured on both sides. Firewall filters blocking TCP port 179 will also prevent BGP; use monitor traffic interface to look for blocked TCP SYNs. For example, if show bgp summary shows Idle or Connect, ping the neighbor from the configured source and run monitor traffic for tcp port 179 — if SYNs never reach the neighbor, investigate routing or ACLs. Another common issue is incorrect neighbor IP: double-check the configured neighbor addresses. After fixing reachability, verify that authentication settings match if MD5/tcp-authentication is in use. Misconception: a configured neighbor IP alone does not guarantee session stability; always verify the underlying TCP path and routing to the update-source. The final step is to confirm routes are exchanged with show bgp summary and show route protocol bgp.

keyIdea.title: BGP Peer Checklist
keyIdea.text: Confirm IP reachability, TCP 179 visibility, correct AS numbers, update-source reachability, and matching authentication before adjusting policies.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.8 › BGP Peering
Triage procedure
  1. Ping the neighbor IP using the configured source: ping <neighbor-ip> source <local-loopback-ip>.
  2. Capture TCP: monitor traffic interface <if> matching "tcp port 179" to ensure SYNs reach the peer.
  3. Confirm AS numbers: show configuration protocols bgp group <group-name>.
  4. Check update-source if using loopbacks and confirm routing to that source IP.
Concrete example
If show bgp summary shows Connect and monitor traffic shows no SYNs, the TCP path is broken — check an intermediate ACL or next-hop route to the neighbor.
Useful commands
ping 203.0.113.2 source 203.0.113.1
monitor traffic interface ge-0/0/0 matching "tcp port 179"
show bgp summary
show configuration protocols bgp group EBGP_PEER
Interpretation tips
  • If ping to neighbor IP fails from the update-source, fix routing before troubleshooting BGP policies.
  • If TCP SYNs reach the peer but BGP still fails, verify AS numbers and authentication.
Key Takeaway

Treat a failed BGP session as a TCP problem first: validate reachability, port visibility, and update-source routing before touching import/export policies.

screens.title: Routes not advertised or received
screens.eyebrow: Core Concept — BGP Route Advertisement Issues
screens.narratorSegment: When BGP peers are established but routes are missing on either side, analysis should pivot to export/import policies, route origin, and next-hop reachability. Start by confirming the route exists locally with show route and then check show configuration policy-options to inspect export rules. If an intended route does not appear on the neighbor, ensure it is permitted by the export policy. For iBGP topologies, a frequent pitfall is next-hop reachability: an iBGP speaker may forward a route with a next-hop that peers cannot reach; next-hop-self can remedy this by setting the advertising router as the next hop. Use set protocols bgp group <group-name> next-hop-self when appropriate. Also check route origin: make sure the route is active in the local RIB before exporting. Another source of lost routes is import policies on the remote side — confirm the neighbor is allowed to install the received routes. A concrete example: eBGP learned prefixes present in show route but not in the internal iBGP peer because an export policy on the eBGP router omitted them. Fix by adjusting policy and verifying with show route protocol bgp and show bgp neighbor <ip> received-routes or policy counters. Misconception: changing policies without verifying counters can hide whether packets or routes were evaluated; add counters to policy terms to observe hits. The closing question: do your peers have routes because of policy, or is next-hop reachability blocking installation?

keyIdea.text: Verify local route presence, export/import policy permits, next-hop reachability, and use next-hop-self for iBGP where needed; add counters to policies to confirm matches.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.8 › BGP Advertisement
Comparison: Export vs Import Issues
Export-side problem
A route present in local RIB but not sent to neighbor because export policy denies it. Use show configuration policy-options and add counters to terms to confirm hits.
Import-side problem
Neighbor sends prefixes but the local import policy rejects them. Verify show bgp neighbor <ip> received-routes or policy counters on the receiving side.
Next-hop issue
iBGP peers may receive routes with a next-hop they cannot reach. Use next-hop-self on the advertising neighbor or ensure next-hop is reachable via the IGP.
Commands & example
show route
show route protocol bgp
show bgp summary
show configuration policy-options
set protocols bgp group EBGP_PEER next-hop-self
Practical tip

Add count counters to policy terms and then run show configuration policy-options or show firewall filter <name> counter to see if traffic or route advertisements match the intended terms before assuming a protocol bug.

Key Takeaway

Missing BGP routes are usually a policy or next-hop issue; verify local presence, policy counters, and next-hop reachability before altering routing protocols.

screens.title: Diagnosing VLAN access vs trunk problems
screens.narratorSegment: When users in a VLAN cannot communicate across a link, the difference between an access-port problem and a trunking problem determines your first checks. Start by confirming host IP, subnet mask, and default gateway to avoid chasing non-network issues. If a host can reach only its local VLAN peers, check the access-port assignment on the switch and whether the switch learned the MAC address on the expected interface. If traffic should cross a trunk, verify the trunk is up and carrying the expected VLANs. Use simple verification commands to build a hypothesis: confirm VLAN definitions on both devices, examine the trunk configuration and VLAN members, and check interface status for physical problems. A recurring real-world mistake is treating a trunk as an access link; another is assuming the switch will automatically add missing VLANs across a trunk. In practice, you will often fix the issue by adding the missing VLAN to the trunk or correcting the interface mode. For example, after discovering VLAN 20 is not a member on one side of a trunk, you would add that VLAN and commit. The investigative sequence—host addressing, VLAN membership, MAC learning, trunk status, and physical link—reduces wasted effort and isolates whether the problem is Layer 2 learning, trunking, or host configuration. As you proceed, ask: does the switch see the host MAC, and does the trunk carry the VLAN? That question points you to the correct fix.

keyIdea.text: Host addressing → VLAN membership → MAC table → trunk config → physical link up. This ordered approach isolates common VLAN/trunk faults quickly.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter: Troubleshooting › Diagnosing VLAN & Trunks
Diagnosing VLAN access vs trunk problems
Follow an ordered check list to isolate access-port faults from trunk misconfiguration.
Core Concept
Comparison: Access port vs Trunk
Access Port

Carries a single VLAN. Check host IP, VLAN membership and MAC learning on the interface.

Mnemonic: single lane
Trunk

Carries multiple VLANs. Verify allowed VLAN list, native VLAN and physical link state.

Mnemonic: multi-lane
Quick verification commands
show configuration vlans
show configuration interfaces ge-0/0/0
show interfaces ge-0/0/0 terse
show ethernet-switching table
Diagnostic flow and example
Follow these steps, confirm after each step before changing configuration.
  1. Confirm host IP, mask, and gateway on both ends.
  2. Check switch VLAN definition with show configuration vlans.
  3. Verify trunk membership and native VLAN; add missing VLANs if needed.
  4. Confirm MAC learning with show ethernet-switching table.
  5. Check physical link and errors with show interfaces terse.
Key Takeaway

Diagnose in order: addressing, VLAN presence, MAC learning, trunk membership, and physical link. This avoids unnecessary changes.

screens.title: Native VLAN mismatches and MAC table clues
screens.narratorSegment: A native VLAN mismatch is one of those subtle Layer 2 mistakes that often looks like intermittent connectivity. The native VLAN is the untagged VLAN on an 802.1Q trunk. If one side of a trunk treats VLAN 10 as native and the other side treats VLAN 1 as native, untagged frames will be delivered to the wrong VLAN or dropped. A practical symptom is that some hosts communicate locally yet fail across the trunk for a specific VLAN. Use the MAC address table to see where the switch learned a host's MAC. If the MAC is learned on the wrong port or VLAN, traffic will never reach the intended destination. The investigative steps are: confirm native-vlan-id settings on both trunk endpoints, validate the trunk's allowed VLAN list, and review the ethernet-switching table for MAC entries and corresponding ports. A common misconception is that tagged VLAN traffic is unaffected by native mismatch; in reality, the untagged traffic and some neighbor discovery frames might be lost or misdirected. Fixes often involve explicitly setting the same native VLAN on both sides or reconfiguring hosts to tag frames when necessary. Always confirm changes by checking the MAC table and testing ping between representative hosts. Finally, document the final native VLAN choices so future engineers do not reintroduce the mismatch.

The investigative steps are: confirm native-vlan-id settings on both trunk endpoints, validate the trunk's allowed VLAN list, and review the ethernet-switching table for MAC entries and corresponding ports. A common misconception is that tagged VLAN traffic is unaffected by native mismatch; in reality, the untagged traffic and some neighbor discovery frames might be lost or misdirected. Fixes often involve explicitly setting the same native VLAN on both sides or reconfiguring hosts to tag frames when necessary. Always confirm changes by checking the MAC table and testing ping between representative hosts. Finally, document the final native VLAN choices so future engineers do not reintroduce the mismatch.

keyIdea.title: Native VLAN rule
keyIdea.text: Native VLAN must match on both trunk endpoints; use the MAC table to validate where traffic is learned and to confirm the fix.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter: Troubleshooting › Native VLAN & MAC table
Native VLAN mismatches and MAC table clues
Use the MAC table and trunk native-vlan-id to find misdirected or dropped untagged traffic.
Step-by-step checks
  1. Check trunk native VLAN on both switches: show configuration interfaces <int> | display set | match "native-vlan-id".
  2. Verify allowed VLAN list on trunk endpoints.
  3. Inspect the MAC table for the affected host: show ethernet-switching table.
  4. If MAC learned on unexpected port or VLAN, trace where the frame arrived and correct the configuration.
  5. After correcting, flush the MAC entry or wait for re-learning, then retest connectivity.
Example commands
show configuration interfaces ge-0/0/0 | display set | match "native-vlan-id"
show configuration interfaces ge-0/0/0
show ethernet-switching table | match aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff
show interfaces ge-0/0/0 terse
Analogy

Think of a trunk as a postbox with some envelopes tagged for different recipients. The native VLAN is the untagged envelope. If the post office decodes untagged mail under the wrong recipient, the message never reaches the intended person.

Common mistake

Assuming only tagged traffic is affected; untagged control frames or guest VLAN traffic can be misdelivered.

Key Takeaway

Match native VLANs on both ends. Use MAC learning as a reliable indicator of where frames actually arrived.

screens.title: Diagnosing STP: blocked ports and unexpected topology
screens.narratorSegment: Spanning Tree Protocol prevents loops but can also block legitimate paths if misconfigured. The primary checks are: verify which device is the root bridge, confirm bridge priorities, and inspect port roles and states. Start with the bridge summary to confirm which switch won the election and whether that matches your design intent. If a less-desirable switch is root, adjust bridge-priority to elect the correct root. Next, examine port roles and states: a port in Alternate or Backup state is blocked and will not forward user traffic. Investigate why a port is blocked — sometimes BPDU Guard or BPDU Filter applied on an inter-switch link can suppress BPDUs and lead to unstable decisions. Another important operational feature is configuring edge ports (PortFast) for access links to end hosts; edge ports avoid temporary blocking during link up, but they must not be enabled on inter-switch links. A common misconception is that disabling STP speeds up forwarding; in fact, disabling or misapplying BPDU filtering can cause loops and broadcast storms. Use commands such as show spanning-tree bridge and show spanning-tree interface to inspect root, priorities, and per-port roles. If you see unexpected blocked ports, trace the path, consider adjusting priorities or moving edge flags off inter-switch links, and validate with traffic tests. Always document your intended root and edge design so STP behaves predictably after maintenance.

keyIdea.title: STP root planning
keyIdea.text: Plan and enforce a stable root bridge; use port roles and edge settings only in appropriate places to avoid blocked important links or loops.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter: Troubleshooting › STP Troubleshooting
Diagnosing STP: blocked ports and unexpected topology
Inspect root bridge, port roles, and BPDU-related features to find blocked or looped paths.
Key checks
  • Confirm root bridge: show spanning-tree bridge.
  • Check per-port roles and state: show spanning-tree interface.
  • Look for BPDU Guard/Filter on inter-switch links that may block BPDUs.
  • Verify edge port configuration only on access ports: set protocols stp interface <if> edge.
Example fixes
# Set expected root priority (lower value preferred)
set protocols stp bridge-priority 28672
# Configure an access port as edge only when connecting a host
set protocols stp interface ge-0/0/5 edge
# Remove BPDU filter from inter-switch link
delete protocols stp interface ge-0/0/1 bpdu-filter
Common symptom and resolution

Symptom: A legitimate uplink is blocked after an upgrade. Resolution: confirm wrong root election or accidental edge/BPDU filter on that link then correct priority or remove edge setting.

Misconception

Don't enable edge on inter-switch links to speed convergence — that can create loops when links flapping occur.

Pro Tip

Plan your root switch explicitly and record priorities so maintenance doesn't inadvertently change election results.

screens.title: Identifying and recovering from loops and storms
screens.narratorSegment: Loops and broadcast storms can saturate a network quickly and cause high C P U on switches. They often occur when STP is disabled, misconfigured, or when a link that should be blocked transitions to forwarding unexpectedly. The immediate diagnostic goal is to isolate the storm domain and stop amplification. First, find which ports are seeing unusually high broadcast or multicast with interface counters and error statistics. Then, look for a sudden surge in MAC table churn using the ethernet-switching table; a rapid change in MAC learning often signals a loop. If you can, shut down the suspected interfaces at switch level to stop the storm while preserving evidence for post-mortem. Once traffic is contained, investigate misapplied STP settings, such as edge flags on inter-switch links or BPDU filtering on a critical trunk. For long-term remediation, ensure proper root placement, avoid manual topology changes without adjusting STP priorities, and use features like BPDU Guard on user-facing ports to protect the network. Remember, disabling STP is never a recommended mitigation except as an emergency containment step in an isolated maintenance window. After restoring topology, validate stability by monitoring MAC learning rates, clearance of broadcast queues, and stable port roles, then document the corrective configuration so the loop does not recur.

keyIdea.text: When a loop occurs, quickly isolate the affected ports to stop the storm, then correct STP misconfigurations and validate steady MAC learning.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter: Troubleshooting › STP Loops & Storms
Identifying and recovering from loops and storms
Contain, diagnose, and prevent — quick mitigation followed by configuration fixes.
Immediate containment steps
  • Identify busy ports: show interfaces extensive.
  • Check MAC churn: show ethernet-switching table | count and recent changes.
  • Isolate by disabling suspect interfaces to stop the storm.
  • Preserve logs and capture samples for forensics before clearing counters.
Useful commands
show interfaces extensive
show ethernet-switching table
show spanning-tree interface
monitor traffic interface ge-0/0/1 no-resolve
Root causes to investigate

Look for disabled STP on critical links, accidental edge configuration on inter-switch ports, or misused BPDU filter/guard settings. Human errors during maintenance are a common source.

Post-recovery validation
  1. Verify stable MAC learning and cleared error counters.
  2. Confirm expected root bridge and port roles.
  3. Document the changes and implement BPDU Guard on user ports.
Why it matters

Loops quickly consume bandwidth and switch CPU. Fast containment preserves service and simplifies diagnosis.

screens.title: Troubleshooting firewall filters and dropped sessions
screens.narratorSegment: Firewall filters are powerful but their ordering and placement can silently drop traffic. When traffic is missing, start by confirming the session exists in the flow or session table for SRX devices. The presence or absence of a session tells you whether stateful processing ever allowed the traffic. Use show security flow session to list active sessions; if the session is absent, packets may be dropped before state establishment. Next, confirm the filter is applied on the intended interface and direction. A frequent mistake is applying an input filter when you intended an output filter. Also inspect term ordering — filters evaluate top-down, so an early deny will mask later permit terms. Adding counters to terms is practical: add count names to suspect terms and watch traffic hit counters with show firewall filter counter. If you need to observe packets, use monitor traffic on the interface to capture ingress and egress frames and verify whether packets reach the device and whether any ICMP unreachable messages are generated. When you identify a misordered deny, move or adjust terms, then re-test. Remember the implicit deny at the end of a filter: if you forget to add an explicit accept for desired traffic, it will be dropped. Finally, after fixes, validate connectivity and confirm sessions appear in the flow table. This workflow—session check, filter placement, term order, counters, and capture—lets you find and fix most firewall filter problems quickly.

keyIdea.title: Filter debug checklist
keyIdea.text: Check session table, filter placement and direction, term order, counters, and then packet captures to pinpoint where traffic is dropped.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter: Troubleshooting › Firewall Filters
Troubleshooting firewall filters and dropped sessions
Use session checks, counters, and packet captures to find where filters block traffic.
Core debugging steps
  1. Check session table: show security flow session.
  2. Confirm filter applied on the correct interface and direction.
  3. Inspect term order and remember implicit deny at the end.
  4. Add counters to suspect terms and observe with show firewall filter <name> counter <counter>.
  5. Capture live packets with monitor traffic interface <int> if needed.
Example commands
show security flow session
show configuration interfaces ge-0/0/0 | display set | match "filter"
show firewall filter MY-FILTER counter
monitor traffic interface ge-0/0/0 matching "tcp port 179"
Example: add a counter term
# add a counter to term 10 to count matches
set firewall family inet filter MY-FILTER term TERM-10 then count TERM10-COUNT
commit
# after traffic runs
show firewall filter MY-FILTER counter TERM10-COUNT
Misconception

Assuming a filter is not applied. Always confirm the interface and direction; an input filter does not affect outbound traffic on the same interface.

Key Takeaway

Use the session table and counters before changing policy logic. Counters and packet captures provide objective evidence of hits and drops.

screens.title: Lab scenario: trunk carries VLAN 10 but VLAN 20 fails
screens.narratorSegment: In the lab scenario two EX switches are connected by a trunk and users in VLAN 10 on Switch A cannot reach users in VLAN 20 on Switch B, while intra-VLAN traffic works locally. Start by verifying VLAN definitions on both switches to ensure VLAN 10 and VLAN 20 exist. Next, check the trunk interface configuration on both sides for interface mode trunk and membership of both VLANs. Confirm physical link state with interface terse. Inspect the native-vlan-id to rule out untagged traffic being misdirected. Use the MAC address table to confirm where hosts' MAC addresses are learned; if a host's MAC appears on the wrong interface or VLAN, that indicates misconfiguration. If the trunk is missing VLAN 20 on Switch A, add VLAN 20 to the trunk's vlan members and commit. The example fix from the chapter is a direct configuration command to include both VLANs in the trunk's vlan members list, then validate that hosts re-learn MACs across the trunk and inter-VLAN routing completes. If the trunk and VLAN membership are correct but traffic still fails, check for firewall filters on the link or switch ACLs, and verify the trunk is not filtered for multicast needed by some protocols. After applying the fix, retest ping between representative hosts and document the correction for future troubleshooting.

keyIdea.title: Hypothesis-driven fixes
keyIdea.text: Form a hypothesis from VLAN and trunk checks, apply a minimal config change, then validate MAC learning and connectivity before documenting the solution.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter: Troubleshooting › Lab: Trunk VLAN mismatch
Lab scenario: trunk carries VLAN 10 but VLAN 20 fails
A practical checklist and the CLI fix you will apply and validate in the lab.
Checklist for the lab
  1. Verify VLANs exist on both switches: show configuration vlans.
  2. Check trunk interface config and allowed VLANs: show configuration interfaces ge-0/0/0.
  3. Confirm physical link is up: show interfaces ge-0/0/0 terse.
  4. Inspect MAC table for hosts in VLAN 10 and VLAN 20.
  5. Form hypothesis and apply minimal fix, then re-validate connectivity.
Commands to run
# Check VLANs
show configuration vlans
# Check trunk config
show configuration interfaces ge-0/0/0
# Check link state
show interfaces ge-0/0/0 terse
# Check MAC learning
show ethernet-switching table
Example fix (if VLAN 20 missing on trunk)
# On Switch A (example fix)
set interfaces ge-0/0/0 unit 0 family ethernet-switching vlan members [ vlan-10 vlan-20 ]
commit
# Validate
show interfaces ge-0/0/0 terse
show ethernet-switching table | match "vlan-20"
Validation steps
  • Confirm MACs for VLAN 20 are learned across the trunk.
  • Ping between representative hosts in VLAN 10 and VLAN 20 after the fix.
  • Document the change and rationale.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Here are three compact concepts to keep top of mind when troubleshooting routing and switching on Juniper devices. First, VLAN trunking requires that the VLAN be defined on both switches and explicitly allowed on the trunk; a missing VLAN on one side is a frequent cause of cross-VLAN failures. Second, Spanning Tree Protocol must be intentionally designed: pick a stable root bridge and apply edge or BPDU features only where appropriate to prevent blocked core links or loops. Third, firewall filters process terms top-down and include an implicit deny at the end; use counters and the session table to objectively confirm whether the device ever established state for the traffic. Keep these concepts as troubleshooting heuristics: verify definitions and membership, confirm control-plane elections and roles, and use counters and session state to prove the packet path. When in doubt, form a hypothesis, apply a small change, validate with show commands, and document the result so the learning is preserved.

Module 8 › Chapter: Troubleshooting › Key Concepts
Key Concepts
Three quick definitions to recall during troubleshooting.
VLAN Trunking
Carry multiple VLANs across one link; both ends must define and allow the same VLANs to pass traffic correctly.
Spanning Tree Protocol
Prevents Layer 2 loops by blocking redundant paths. Root bridge selection and port roles determine which links forward.
Firewall Filter
Policy terms evaluate top-down with an implicit deny at the end. Use counters and the session table to confirm which terms match traffic.
Summary

When troubleshooting, verify definitions, check control-plane roles, and gather objective evidence such as MAC entries, sessions, and counters before changing configurations.

screens.title: What to Remember
screens.narratorSegment: Keep three operational reminders at hand. First, native VLAN mismatches cause unexpected untagged traffic drops — always verify native-vlan-id on both ends of a trunk. Second, MAC address tables are your most direct evidence of where frames are being learned and can indicate miswired or misconfigured ports. Third, for firewall filters, remember that a missed permit or a misplaced deny is often the cause of traffic failures — adding counters and checking the session table will quickly show whether packets ever reached the device. These reminders combine configuration checks with objective validation, helping you avoid guesswork and resolve problems reliably. When you finish a fix, document the change, test with representative hosts, and re-run the same show commands to confirm the network now behaves as intended. What to Remember

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we focus on practical troubleshooting patterns you will use every day with Junos devices. You will learn to form a hypothesis, collect evidence with show commands, inspect control-plane exchanges like OSPF LSAs and BGP TCP sessions, and validate fixes. For example, if an OSPF neighbor is stuck in ExStart, the immediate checks include interface status, MTU, area ID, and firewall filters blocking multicast. Each technique pairs a command such as show ospf neighbor, show interfaces extensive, or monitor traffic with a reasoning step that tells you what to expect. We emphasize common misconceptions too — for instance, missing routes in the RIB are not always a routing-protocol bug; they can be the result of passive interfaces, export policies, or implicit deny in firewall filters. By the end of these lessons you'll be able to triage adjacencies, peering, trunk mismatches, STP roles, and filter term order confidently and document the fix. Start by learning the core checks and commands, then practice the scenario-based steps to build reliable troubleshooting muscle memory.

This chapter trains you to diagnose and resolve the most frequent routing and switching faults on Juniper gear. First, you will learn to detect and fix OSPF adjacency and LSA issues — for example, recognizing the impact of an MTU mismatch or a passive interface on adjacency formation. Second, you will be able to bring up BGP peers reliably by verifying TCP reachability, AS numbers, and update-source settings, and by checking policy-based import/export mistakes. Third, you will verify VLAN membership and trunk configuration to restore inter-VLAN traffic and fix native VLAN mismatches that silently drop traffic. Fourth, you will inspect Spanning Tree behavior to identify incorrect root bridge election or blocked ports causing unexpected paths. Each objective pairs concrete Junos commands with a troubleshooting mindset so you can find the root cause quickly and test your fixes. A common misconception is to change configuration without first validating control-plane evidence; these objectives emphasize collecting show output and forming a hypothesis before committing a fix.

Beyond the core protocol checks, this chapter teaches supporting skills that make troubleshooting effective and repeatable. You will learn to examine Junos outputs such as show ospf database to verify LSAs, show bgp summary to confirm TCP sessions, and show security flow session to observe SRX session state. You will practice adding counters to firewall filter terms and using monitor traffic to capture packet-level evidence. Another objective is to form a clear hypothesis and document the findings and the fix — a habit that reduces repeat incidents. For example, after resolving a native VLAN mismatch you should record the original trunk settings, the corrective set command, and the verification output. A common misconception is to rely solely on a single show command; we stress combining multiple outputs — interface, protocol, and policy — to paint an accurate picture before committing changes.

When an OSPF neighbor fails to reach Full, start by defining the claim: adjacency formation requires IP connectivity, matching area IDs, compatible network types, identical authentication and MTU, and that nothing in the path blocks OSPF packets. A concrete example is an adjacency stuck in ExStart. ExStart often points to an MTU mismatch preventing Database Description exchange. To check, run show interfaces <interface> detail and compare MTU on both peers; also confirm interface is up/up. Then run show ospf neighbor to observe the state and show ospf database to review LSA exchange progress. Another common cause is passive-interface misconfiguration: passive prevents Hello exchange and LSA propagation. If neighbors are configured with different network types — for instance one side set to point-to-point and the other left as broadcast — adjacency can fail or remain in 2-Way. Also confirm firewall filters are not blocking OSPF multicast addresses 224.0.0.5 or 224.0.0.6. A typical remediation sequence is: validate interface and MTU, remove unintended passive, set matching interface-type, and then clear ospf neighbor or reset the interface to force reformation. Misconception check: do not change area IDs or authentication without collecting evidence; that can create new failures. Takeaway: verify MTU and interface settings first, then inspect LSA and neighbor states.

When OSPF routes are missing from the routing table, the problem often lies downstream from adjacency formation: inspect the LSA database, router IDs, and whether interfaces are inadvertently passive. Begin with show route protocol ospf to identify which prefixes were learned and which are absent. Then use show ospf database to see if LSAs for those networks exist locally; missing LSAs indicate the network was never advertised or was filtered. Router ID conflicts can prevent proper LSA acceptance or cause confusing behavior — verify uniqueness with show ospf overview. Passive interfaces stop Hello exchanges and prevent LSA advertisement for networks on that interface; check configuration for unintended passive statements. Another frequent policy-level cause is firewall filters blocking LSAs or multicast addresses 224.0.0.5 and 224.0.0.6. A concrete example: an internal network not appearing because the interface was set to passive in the area configuration. Fix by removing the passive flag for that interface and verifying LSA injection with show ospf database and then show route protocol ospf. Misconception check: a missing OSPF route in the RIB does not always mean the LSA was incorrect — it can be suppressed by policy, rejected by route selection, or overridden by a more specific static route. The takeaway: correlate adjacency, LSA, and policy outputs to find the true cause.

When BGP does not show an Established state, treat the issue as a TCP reachability and configuration verification task. Start by confirming basic reachability with ping to the neighbor IP and by testing TCP port 179 with a packet capture or monitor traffic filter. A common operational check is to ensure the correct AS numbers are configured for each peer; mismatched AS numbers will prevent session establishment. If you use loopback interfaces as update-source, verify that the neighbor reaches that loopback via the control-plane and that update-source is configured on both sides. Firewall filters blocking TCP port 179 will also prevent BGP; use monitor traffic interface to look for blocked TCP SYNs. For example, if show bgp summary shows Idle or Connect, ping the neighbor from the configured source and run monitor traffic for tcp port 179 — if SYNs never reach the neighbor, investigate routing or ACLs. Another common issue is incorrect neighbor IP: double-check the configured neighbor addresses. After fixing reachability, verify that authentication settings match if MD5/tcp-authentication is in use. Misconception: a configured neighbor IP alone does not guarantee session stability; always verify the underlying TCP path and routing to the update-source. The final step is to confirm routes are exchanged with show bgp summary and show route protocol bgp.

When BGP peers are established but routes are missing on either side, analysis should pivot to export/import policies, route origin, and next-hop reachability. Start by confirming the route exists locally with show route and then check show configuration policy-options to inspect export rules. If an intended route does not appear on the neighbor, ensure it is permitted by the export policy. For iBGP topologies, a frequent pitfall is next-hop reachability: an iBGP speaker may forward a route with a next-hop that peers cannot reach; next-hop-self can remedy this by setting the advertising router as the next hop. Use set protocols bgp group <group-name> next-hop-self when appropriate. Also check route origin: make sure the route is active in the local RIB before exporting. Another source of lost routes is import policies on the remote side — confirm the neighbor is allowed to install the received routes. A concrete example: eBGP learned prefixes present in show route but not in the internal iBGP peer because an export policy on the eBGP router omitted them. Fix by adjusting policy and verifying with show route protocol bgp and show bgp neighbor <ip> received-routes or policy counters. Misconception: changing policies without verifying counters can hide whether packets or routes were evaluated; add counters to policy terms to observe hits. The closing question: do your peers have routes because of policy, or is next-hop reachability blocking installation?

When users in a VLAN cannot communicate across a link, the difference between an access-port problem and a trunking problem determines your first checks. Start by confirming host IP, subnet mask, and default gateway to avoid chasing non-network issues. If a host can reach only its local VLAN peers, check the access-port assignment on the switch and whether the switch learned the MAC address on the expected interface. If traffic should cross a trunk, verify the trunk is up and carrying the expected VLANs. Use simple verification commands to build a hypothesis: confirm VLAN definitions on both devices, examine the trunk configuration and VLAN members, and check interface status for physical problems. A recurring real-world mistake is treating a trunk as an access link; another is assuming the switch will automatically add missing VLANs across a trunk. In practice, you will often fix the issue by adding the missing VLAN to the trunk or correcting the interface mode. For example, after discovering VLAN 20 is not a member on one side of a trunk, you would add that VLAN and commit. The investigative sequence—host addressing, VLAN membership, MAC learning, trunk status, and physical link—reduces wasted effort and isolates whether the problem is Layer 2 learning, trunking, or host configuration. As you proceed, ask: does the switch see the host MAC, and does the trunk carry the VLAN? That question points you to the correct fix.

A native VLAN mismatch is one of those subtle Layer 2 mistakes that often looks like intermittent connectivity. The native VLAN is the untagged VLAN on an 802.1Q trunk. If one side of a trunk treats VLAN 10 as native and the other side treats VLAN 1 as native, untagged frames will be delivered to the wrong VLAN or dropped. A practical symptom is that some hosts communicate locally yet fail across the trunk for a specific VLAN. Use the MAC address table to see where the switch learned a host's MAC. If the MAC is learned on the wrong port or VLAN, traffic will never reach the intended destination. The investigative steps are: confirm native-vlan-id settings on both trunk endpoints, validate the trunk's allowed VLAN list, and review the ethernet-switching table for MAC entries and corresponding ports. A common misconception is that tagged VLAN traffic is unaffected by native mismatch; in reality, the untagged traffic and some neighbor discovery frames might be lost or misdirected. Fixes often involve explicitly setting the same native VLAN on both sides or reconfiguring hosts to tag frames when necessary. Always confirm changes by checking the MAC table and testing ping between representative hosts. Finally, document the final native VLAN choices so future engineers do not reintroduce the mismatch.

Spanning Tree Protocol prevents loops but can also block legitimate paths if misconfigured. The primary checks are: verify which device is the root bridge, confirm bridge priorities, and inspect port roles and states. Start with the bridge summary to confirm which switch won the election and whether that matches your design intent. If a less-desirable switch is root, adjust bridge-priority to elect the correct root. Next, examine port roles and states: a port in Alternate or Backup state is blocked and will not forward user traffic. Investigate why a port is blocked — sometimes BPDU Guard or BPDU Filter applied on an inter-switch link can suppress BPDUs and lead to unstable decisions. Another important operational feature is configuring edge ports (PortFast) for access links to end hosts; edge ports avoid temporary blocking during link up, but they must not be enabled on inter-switch links. A common misconception is that disabling STP speeds up forwarding; in fact, disabling or misapplying BPDU filtering can cause loops and broadcast storms. Use commands such as show spanning-tree bridge and show spanning-tree interface to inspect root, priorities, and per-port roles. If you see unexpected blocked ports, trace the path, consider adjusting priorities or moving edge flags off inter-switch links, and validate with traffic tests. Always document your intended root and edge design so STP behaves predictably after maintenance.

Loops and broadcast storms can saturate a network quickly and cause high C P U on switches. They often occur when STP is disabled, misconfigured, or when a link that should be blocked transitions to forwarding unexpectedly. The immediate diagnostic goal is to isolate the storm domain and stop amplification. First, find which ports are seeing unusually high broadcast or multicast with interface counters and error statistics. Then, look for a sudden surge in MAC table churn using the ethernet-switching table; a rapid change in MAC learning often signals a loop. If you can, shut down the suspected interfaces at switch level to stop the storm while preserving evidence for post-mortem. Once traffic is contained, investigate misapplied STP settings, such as edge flags on inter-switch links or BPDU filtering on a critical trunk. For long-term remediation, ensure proper root placement, avoid manual topology changes without adjusting STP priorities, and use features like BPDU Guard on user-facing ports to protect the network. Remember, disabling STP is never a recommended mitigation except as an emergency containment step in an isolated maintenance window. After restoring topology, validate stability by monitoring MAC learning rates, clearance of broadcast queues, and stable port roles, then document the corrective configuration so the loop does not recur.

Firewall filters are powerful but their ordering and placement can silently drop traffic. When traffic is missing, start by confirming the session exists in the flow or session table for SRX devices. The presence or absence of a session tells you whether stateful processing ever allowed the traffic. Use show security flow session to list active sessions; if the session is absent, packets may be dropped before state establishment. Next, confirm the filter is applied on the intended interface and direction. A frequent mistake is applying an input filter when you intended an output filter. Also inspect term ordering — filters evaluate top-down, so an early deny will mask later permit terms. Adding counters to terms is practical: add count names to suspect terms and watch traffic hit counters with show firewall filter counter. If you need to observe packets, use monitor traffic on the interface to capture ingress and egress frames and verify whether packets reach the device and whether any ICMP unreachable messages are generated. When you identify a misordered deny, move or adjust terms, then re-test. Remember the implicit deny at the end of a filter: if you forget to add an explicit accept for desired traffic, it will be dropped. Finally, after fixes, validate connectivity and confirm sessions appear in the flow table. This workflow—session check, filter placement, term order, counters, and capture—lets you find and fix most firewall filter problems quickly.

In the lab scenario two EX switches are connected by a trunk and users in VLAN 10 on Switch A cannot reach users in VLAN 20 on Switch B, while intra-VLAN traffic works locally. Start by verifying VLAN definitions on both switches to ensure VLAN 10 and VLAN 20 exist. Next, check the trunk interface configuration on both sides for interface mode trunk and membership of both VLANs. Confirm physical link state with interface terse. Inspect the native-vlan-id to rule out untagged traffic being misdirected. Use the MAC address table to confirm where hosts' MAC addresses are learned; if a host's MAC appears on the wrong interface or VLAN, that indicates misconfiguration. If the trunk is missing VLAN 20 on Switch A, add VLAN 20 to the trunk's vlan members and commit. The example fix from the chapter is a direct configuration command to include both VLANs in the trunk's vlan members list, then validate that hosts re-learn MACs across the trunk and inter-VLAN routing completes. If the trunk and VLAN membership are correct but traffic still fails, check for firewall filters on the link or switch ACLs, and verify the trunk is not filtered for multicast needed by some protocols. After applying the fix, retest ping between representative hosts and document the correction for future troubleshooting.

Here are three compact concepts to keep top of mind when troubleshooting routing and switching on Juniper devices. First, VLAN trunking requires that the VLAN be defined on both switches and explicitly allowed on the trunk; a missing VLAN on one side is a frequent cause of cross-VLAN failures. Second, Spanning Tree Protocol must be intentionally designed: pick a stable root bridge and apply edge or BPDU features only where appropriate to prevent blocked core links or loops. Third, firewall filters process terms top-down and include an implicit deny at the end; use counters and the session table to objectively confirm whether the device ever established state for the traffic. Keep these concepts as troubleshooting heuristics: verify definitions and membership, confirm control-plane elections and roles, and use counters and session state to prove the packet path. When in doubt, form a hypothesis, apply a small change, validate with show commands, and document the result so the learning is preserved.

Keep three operational reminders at hand. First, native VLAN mismatches cause unexpected untagged traffic drops — always verify native-vlan-id on both ends of a trunk. Second, MAC address tables are your most direct evidence of where frames are being learned and can indicate miswired or misconfigured ports. Third, for firewall filters, remember that a missed permit or a misplaced deny is often the cause of traffic failures — adding counters and checking the session table will quickly show whether packets ever reached the device. These reminders combine configuration checks with objective validation, helping you avoid guesswork and resolve problems reliably. When you finish a fix, document the change, test with representative hosts, and re-run the same show commands to confirm the network now behaves as intended. What to Remember means verify native vlans, use mac tables as evidence, and use counters/session checks for firewall troubleshooting.. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.
